indicators.statement: Recognise parents as sources of discipline and character formation.

questions.prompt: What is one constructive purpose of fair discipline at home?
options: To guide children toward safe and responsible choices
To show that children have no value
questions.answer: To guide children toward safe and responsible choices
questions.hint: Think of discipline as guidance for learning.
questions.explanation: Fair, age-appropriate discipline can help children learn responsibility and self-control.
questions.misconception_note: Discipline does not justify violence, humiliation or unsafe treatment.

questions.prompt: Name one positive character quality that a parent or caregiver may help a child develop.
questions.hint: Think of a quality that supports good relationships.
questions.explanation: Caregivers can support character formation through guidance and example.
questions.misconception_note: Children may also learn from other trusted adults and communities.

criteria.description: Examples include honesty, respect, patience, responsibility, kindness or self-control.

questions.prompt: A caregiver explains a household rule and listens to a child's question. What does this show?
options: Guidance can teach understanding and responsibility
questions.answer: Guidance can teach understanding and responsibility
questions.hint: Notice the explanation and listening.
questions.explanation: Clear, respectful guidance helps children understand expectations.
questions.misconception_note: Families and caregivers differ; respect and safety matter.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a parent modelling good character?
options: Keeping a promise and admitting an error
questions.answer: Keeping a promise and admitting an error
questions.hint: Children learn from adults' actions as well as words.
questions.explanation: Adults can demonstrate qualities they encourage in children.
questions.misconception_note: No caregiver is perfect; learning and repair matter.

questions.prompt: How can fair guidance help a child after a mistake?
questions.hint: Consider learning and making things right.
questions.explanation: Constructive discipline focuses on learning and responsible behaviour.
questions.misconception_note: Mistakes should not be met with abuse or humiliation.

criteria.description: It can help the child understand the effect, take responsibility and make a safer or kinder choice next time.

questions.prompt: Which response is consistent with respectful discipline?
options: A calm explanation of a reasonable consequence
questions.answer: A calm explanation of a reasonable consequence
questions.hint: Choose an approach that teaches without harming.
questions.explanation: Respectful guidance is clear, proportionate and safe.
questions.misconception_note: Violence and degrading treatment are not acceptable discipline.

questions.prompt: Match the character quality to an example: (1) honesty; (2) responsibility; (3) respect. A. caring for an agreed task; B. speaking truthfully; C. listening without insulting.
questions.hint: Match each value to the action that shows it.
questions.explanation: Actions can demonstrate character qualities.
questions.misconception_note: Accept other reasonable examples if discussed orally.

questions.prompt: Orally describe one way a caregiver can encourage a child to act responsibly.
questions.hint: Think of guidance that helps a child learn.
questions.explanation: Caregivers can encourage responsible behaviour through support and example.
questions.misconception_note: Accept oral answers; do not assume every learner lives with parents.

criteria.description: A reasonable example such as explaining expectations, modelling responsibility or praising effort.

questions.prompt: A child is upset about a rule. What is a constructive next step for the child?
options: Ask respectfully for an explanation when it is safe
Break something to prove a point
questions.answer: Ask respectfully for an explanation when it is safe
questions.hint: Choose communication that supports understanding and safety.
questions.explanation: Respectful discussion can help children understand expectations.
questions.misconception_note: If a rule or situation feels unsafe, seek help from a trusted adult.

questions.prompt: Why can a caregiver's example influence a child's character?
options: Children may observe and learn patterns of behaviour
Every child must copy every adult action
questions.answer: Children may observe and learn patterns of behaviour
questions.hint: Consider how people learn by watching others.
questions.explanation: Role modelling is one way children learn social and moral behaviour.
questions.misconception_note: Children can think critically and learn from many sources.

questions.prompt: Give one example of a fair household rule that could help form good habits.
questions.hint: Choose a clear and age-appropriate expectation.
questions.explanation: Consistent, fair expectations can support helpful habits.
questions.misconception_note: Rules should be safe, fair and appropriate to a child's age.

criteria.description: A reasonable rule such as putting away shared items, speaking respectfully or following a safe routine.

questions.prompt: What should a child do if discipline at home involves harm or makes them feel unsafe?
options: Tell a trusted adult who can help keep them safe
Keep it secret no matter what
questions.answer: Tell a trusted adult who can help keep them safe
questions.hint: Safety concerns should be shared with someone trustworthy.
questions.explanation: Children deserve safety and should seek help when at risk.
questions.misconception_note: Never normalise abuse or tell a child to remain in danger.

questions.prompt: Which outcome can fair discipline support?
options: The belief that mistakes cannot be repaired
questions.answer: Self-control and understanding of consequences
questions.hint: Choose a learning outcome rather than a harmful effect.
questions.explanation: Fair guidance can help children consider choices and consequences.
questions.misconception_note: Discipline should be supportive, not harmful or discriminatory.

questions.prompt: A caregiver notices a child telling the truth about a mistake. What response best supports character formation?
options: Acknowledge the honesty and guide the child to repair harm
Shame the child for admitting it
Tell the child truth never matters
questions.answer: Acknowledge the honesty and guide the child to repair harm
questions.hint: Reinforce the positive choice and support responsibility.
questions.explanation: Recognising honesty while addressing consequences encourages learning.
questions.misconception_note: Accountability can be kind and constructive.

questions.prompt: Draw a scene showing a caregiver teaching a child a positive character quality through example or fair guidance.
questions.hint: Show what the adult does and how it helps the child learn.
questions.explanation: The drawing represents how guidance or role modelling can shape behaviour.
questions.misconception_note: Assess the idea, not drawing skill or family structure.

criteria.description: A clear scene showing respectful guidance or an adult modelling a positive quality.

questions.prompt: Role-play a calm conversation where a caregiver explains a fair rule and a child responds respectfully with a question.
questions.hint: Use a simple everyday rule and take turns speaking.
questions.explanation: Respectful communication can make guidance clearer.
questions.misconception_note: This is a classroom practice scenario, not a claim about learners' homes.

criteria.description: Both roles listen and speak respectfully

questions.prompt: Name one way a child can show they have learned from fair guidance.
questions.hint: Think of an action that shows learning.
questions.explanation: Character formation is reflected in choices and actions over time.
questions.misconception_note: Allow for different circumstances and learning needs.

criteria.description: Examples: follow a safe rule, apologise, correct a mistake, care for belongings or make a more responsible choice.

questions.prompt: Which statement about character formation is most accurate?
options: It can develop through guidance, example, practice and reflection
It is completed in one day
A child can never change a habit
questions.answer: It can develop through guidance, example, practice and reflection
questions.hint: Think of character as something developed over time.
questions.explanation: Children learn from caregivers and other influences through ongoing experience.
questions.misconception_note: Avoid blaming children or assuming one influence determines everything.

questions.prompt: Explain one positive character quality and give an example of how a parent or caregiver might encourage it safely and fairly.
questions.hint: Connect the quality to a specific action.
questions.explanation: This demonstrates understanding of caregivers' role in character formation.
questions.misconception_note: Assess understanding, not the learner's personal family situation.

criteria.description: Gives a realistic guidance or role-model example

questions.prompt: Which best describes parents' role as sources of discipline and character formation?
options: They can guide, teach and model positive behaviour
They should control every thought a child has
They may use any punishment they choose
questions.answer: They can guide, teach and model positive behaviour
questions.hint: Choose the supportive and balanced description.
questions.explanation: Parents and caregivers can support children's moral learning through guidance and example.
questions.misconception_note: Caregiving authority does not remove children's right to safety and respect.

indicators.content_standard: B5.5.1.1. Appreciate the need to obey and submit to authority

indicators.statement: Explain the need to demonstrate responsible behaviour at home.

questions.prompt: Which action shows responsibility for a shared room?
questions.hint: Consider the people who use it next.
questions.explanation: Putting things away leaves the shared space ready for other people.
options: Leave your items for the next person
Move the items onto someone else’s chair
Put the items you used back in place
questions.answer: Put the items you used back in place

questions.prompt: Ama returns the torch to its usual shelf after using it. Why does this matter?
questions.hint: Think about the next person who needs light.
questions.explanation: Returning a shared item makes it easy for another person to find it.
options: Nobody else can use it now
Her family will need another torch
Someone else can find it when needed
The shelf will belong only to Ama
questions.answer: Someone else can find it when needed

questions.prompt: Give an example of something a child can learn by watching a responsible adult at home.
questions.hint: Choose a small action that is safe to copy.
questions.explanation: For example, watching an adult return a borrowed bowl can teach a child to look after other people’s things.

criteria.description: Explains what a child could learn.

questions.prompt: Kojo’s grandfather admits he has misplaced a key and helps look for it. Which behaviour can Kojo copy?
questions.hint: Notice what the grandfather does after the mistake.
questions.explanation: Owning a mistake and helping to put it right are ways to be accountable.
options: Wait for a reward before helping
Admit mistakes and help put them right
Let younger relatives take the blame
questions.answer: Admit mistakes and help put them right

questions.prompt: What does it mean to take responsibility for a family task? Give a simple example.
questions.hint: Choose something a learner can reasonably do.
questions.explanation: Someone agrees to do a task and follows through, such as feeding a pet with an adult’s guidance.

criteria.description: Describes following through on a duty.

questions.prompt: A pupil agreed to set the table but must finish homework at the same time. What should the pupil do?
questions.hint: How can the family plan when someone is busy?
questions.explanation: Speaking early allows the family to agree on a change and still get the meal ready.
options: Assume a sibling will notice and help
Say the table is ready when it is not
Explain the clash and agree on a plan
questions.answer: Explain the clash and agree on a plan

questions.prompt: Esi puts dirty cups into the washing area without being asked. Explain one benefit for her family.
questions.hint: Who is helped by her action?
questions.explanation: The cups are ready for washing, and the family can use the table again.

criteria.description: Links the benefit to a household need.

questions.prompt: Tell a partner how learning a small home duty can help a person become a responsible adult.
questions.hint: Think about a habit that grows with practice.
questions.explanation: A child who remembers a daily duty practises planning and following through on commitments.

questions.prompt: A child offers to carry a load but finds it too heavy. What shows responsible judgement?
questions.hint: Consider how to help while keeping everyone safe.
questions.explanation: Telling an adult allows the load to be divided or carried by someone able to manage it.
options: Carry the load to avoid criticism
Explain and ask for safe help
Give the whole load to a younger child
Hide the load behind the door
questions.answer: Explain and ask for safe help

questions.prompt: Plan two jobs for a family preparing for visitors. Show how a child and an adult could share them fairly.
questions.hint: Consider what each person can safely manage.
questions.explanation: A child can arrange seats or cups while an adult handles hot food. The jobs help the family prepare together.

criteria.description: Explains how the tasks help the household.

questions.prompt: Which reason for keeping a promise at home still applies when no one is watching?
questions.hint: Consider what another person may be counting on.
questions.explanation: A promise helps people plan. Keeping it makes your word dependable.
questions.answer: Others rely on the promise

questions.prompt: Draw two scenes showing a shared item before and after a child cares for it. Explain the benefit.
questions.hint: Think of a book, tool or game used by several relatives.
questions.explanation: For example, a torn book can be shown being repaired with help so the next reader can use it.

questions.prompt: A relative always puts tools away carefully. Describe how to follow that example with your own school materials.
questions.hint: Transfer the habit to something you use.
questions.explanation: A pupil can return pencils to a case after work so the materials are safe and ready for the next day.

criteria.description: Names an action modelled on the example.

questions.prompt: Act out a child telling a caregiver that an agreed job is unfinished. Include a practical way forward.
questions.hint: Think about honesty and the next step.
questions.explanation: The child explains what happened and agrees with the caregiver on when or how to finish.

questions.prompt: A child says, “I only help at home to avoid punishment.” Give a different reason and show it in a household example.
questions.hint: Think of someone who depends on the help.
questions.explanation: Helping can express care. Setting out a seat for a visiting relative makes the person welcome.

criteria.description: Connects it to a specific example.

questions.prompt: A sibling has forgotten a shared duty. Explain how to remind them respectfully without doing the entire job for them.
questions.hint: Consider what a helpful reminder sounds like.
questions.explanation: Name the agreed task calmly and ask whether the sibling needs help planning the next step.

criteria.description: Leaves room for the sibling to take responsibility.

questions.prompt: Create a simple plan for looking after a borrowed household item. Include what to do if it is damaged.
questions.hint: Think about using, storing and returning it.
questions.explanation: Use it carefully, return it as agreed, and tell the owner promptly about damage so a repair can be arranged.

criteria.description: Explains an honest response to damage.

questions.prompt: In a pair, play a caregiver and a learner choosing a safe job together. Show how the adult models responsibility.
questions.hint: Let the adult show or explain the task before asking for help.
questions.explanation: The caregiver demonstrates a suitable task and listens to questions. The learner confirms what to do and when.

criteria.description: Agrees on a safe duty the learner can complete.

questions.prompt: Two children take turns on a safe chore. One repeatedly forgets. Suggest a fair plan and explain how to check whether it helps.
questions.hint: Consider a reminder and a way to review it.
questions.explanation: A shared timetable can show whose turn it is. After a week the children can check whether each completed the agreed turns.

criteria.description: Proposes a fair and workable plan.
Explains how the children can evaluate it.

questions.prompt: Write a short paragraph on becoming a dependable adult. Use a responsible action you can practise at home now and explain why it matters.
questions.hint: Join a present action to a future habit.
questions.explanation: Keeping an agreed household duty develops reliability. People learn that they can plan around your word.

criteria.description: Explains how it develops dependable behaviour.
